content: We classified the reflex testing strategy into two categories: clinic-based reflex testing and laboratory-based reflex testing. Laboratory-based HCV reflex testing was defined as a testing algorithm that requires only a single clinical encounter, during which one blood sample or specimen is collected and sent to the laboratory for further analysis. In contrast, clinic-based reflex testing was defined as a testing algorithm that also involves a single clinical encounter but includes an initial rapid diagnostic HCV antibody test followed by a second blood draw during the same visit for individuals who test positive for HCV antibodies, to assess for viremia. The primary intervention examined was one-step laboratory-based reflex confirmatory viral load (VL) testing. This was compared to the traditional multi-step confirmatory testing strategy, which involves standard HCV viral load testing after a second clinic visit following a positive HCV antibody test. Additionally, we collected data on clinic-based reflex sample collection testing strategies, although none of these studies included a non-reflex comparison group. The primary outcomes assessed were the uptake of HCV RNA viral load testing, linkage to care, and initiation of treatment. Secondary outcomes included the time required for various steps in the HCV care cascade, such as the time from HCV antibody testing to RNA testing, RNA sample collection to RNA testing, RNA testing to the availability of results for the patient, RNA testing to linkage to care, and linkage to care to treatment initiation. We also evaluated the feasibility of the reflex testing strategy. Data on cascade outcome proportions were pooled for studies comparing one-step reflex testing to traditional multi-step confirmatory testing using random-effects meta-analysis. Confidence intervals were calculated using the exact binomial (Clopper-Pearson) method, and the Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation was applied to stabilize variance. We assessed the proportion of patients at each step of the care cascade to evaluate attrition for those undergoing reflex testing, including studies without a non-reflex comparator arm. Analyses were conducted for all populations combined and for subgroups such as people who inject drugs, homeless individuals, people living with HCV, hospitalized patients, baby boomers, and the general or mixed population. The relative risk (RR) of RNA testing and treatment uptake was calculated and pooled in a random-effects meta-analysis for studies with within-study comparisons of one-step reflex versus traditional multi-step HCV testing strategies. Small-study effects, a potential marker for publication bias, were tested using a regression-based Egger test. Statistical heterogeneity between studies was measured using the I² statistic. The risk of bias for each study was assessed using a modified version of the Ottawa-Newcastle tool for observational studies reporting binary outcomes. Disagreements between initial assessors were resolved by consulting a third author. The strength of evidence was graded as high, moderate, low, or very low based on risk of bias, consistency of results, directness of evidence, and precision of effect estimates. High confidence indicated that further research was unlikely to change the estimate of effect, while very low confidence indicated insufficient evidence to draw conclusions. A total of 10,750 studies/abstracts were screened, with 30 additional studies identified through reference screening. Nineteen studies on clinic-based reflex testing using HCV point-of-care viral load testing were also included. Of the 51 studies analyzed, 35% were conducted in the United States, 18% in Spain, and 10% in the United Kingdom. Only 18% were conducted in lowand middle-income countries, while 82% were conducted in high-income countries. Most studies (82%) were published after 2018, and all were either cross-sectional or cohort studies, with no randomized controlled trials. Among the included studies, 63% used laboratory-based reflex testing, and 37% used clinic-based reflex testing. Nine of the laboratory-based reflex testing studies included a non-reflex comparison group, while none of the clinic-based reflex testing studies did. For laboratory-based reflex testing, 96% of patients screened as antibody-positive initiated HCV RNA testing, 58% were diagnosed with HCV infection, 77% were linked to care, and 45% initiated treatment. In comparison, for non-reflex testing, 68% of antibody-positive patients initiated RNA testing, 63% were diagnosed with HCV, 63% were linked to care, and 67% initiated treatment. Reflex testing significantly reduced the turnaround time from antibody testing to RNA sample collection to zero days, as it was a one-step process. The time from RNA testing to treatment initiation ranged from 52 to 83 days for reflex testing, compared to 70 days for non-reflex testing. For clinic-based reflex testing, 94% of antibody-positive patients initiated RNA testing, 67% were diagnosed with HCV, 75% were linked to care, and 83% initiated treatment. The median turnaround time from RNA sample collection to viral load testing was zero days in most studies, with treatment initiation occurring within 0 to 57 days. The findings demonstrate that reflex testing, whether laboratoryor clinic-based, improves the uptake of HCV RNA testing and facilitates linkage to care and treatment. Laboratory-based reflex testing was particularly effective in increasing service uptake compared to non-reflex testing. Reflex testing strategies, which often use a single blood sample for both screening and viral load testing, significantly reduce turnaround times and prevent loss to follow-up by eliminating the need for a second clinic visit. These results highlight the feasibility and effectiveness of reflex testing in improving the HCV care cascade.
